chunks: What Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allāh narrated, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Faḍāla, from Mu'āwiya ibn Wahb, who said:
I asked Abī 'Abd Allāh (peace be upon him): "What is the minimum [distance] at which prayer is shortened?" He replied: "A barīd going and a barīd returning."

[Al-Ṭūsī:] With the qualification that what I say regarding this is: shortening is obligatory when the distance is eight farsakhs, and when it is four farsakhs one has the choice — if he wishes he may complete [the prayer] and if he wishes he may shorten it. And that which indicates this — I mean the permissibility of shortening at four farsakhs [is as follows]...

key_terms.التَّقْصِيرُ: shortening (qasr) — reducing four-rak'a prayers to two during qualifying travel
key_terms.الْخِيَارُ: choice/option — the traveler's discretionary right to choose between full and shortened prayer at the threshold distance
key_terms.بَرِيدٌ: barīd — traditional postal/distance unit equal to four farsakhs (approx. 22 km); two barīds (one going, one returning) = eight farsakhs
key_terms.فَرَاسِخَ: farsakhs — plural of farsakh, a classical distance unit of approx. 5.5–6 km

ai.seo_question: What is the minimum travel distance in Shia fiqh at which qasr (shortened) prayer becomes obligatory?
ai.summary: Mu'āwiya ibn Wahb asks Imam al-Ṣādiq (AS) about the minimum travel distance triggering qasr (shortened) prayer; the Imam answers 'a barīd going and a barīd returning' (two barīds = eight farsakhs total, approx. 44 km). Al-Ṭūsī then appends his own legal analysis, distinguishing between the distance at which shortening is obligatory (eight farsakhs) and the distance at which it becomes optional (four farsakhs), with the text cut off before his cited evidence.
